extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in UK celebrity news, comedy controversies, and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether comedic material that references or ridicules disabled individuals (especially children) is acceptable, and how media/platforms and the public should respond. Covers arguments about harm, discrimination, broadcaster responsibility, and cancellation/reporting actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use a child with complex needs as a joke subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Katie Price: 'Having to use my son with complex needs and can't defend himself for a joke, makes this man a disgusting human being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a vulnerable child (who cannot defend themselves) as the butt of jokes is presented as morally unacceptable and grounds for outrage and calls for cancellation; examples include calling out the comedian publicly and urging followers to report the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ridiculing people for disability (double-standard concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Price argued: 'They are saying it is ok to ridicule people - even children - for disability in a way they would not dare over race or sexual orientation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets an evaluative standard that disability should not be singled out for ridicule, especially where other protected characteristics would be treated differently; broadcasters or platforms enabling such ridicule are criticized as endorsing discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability through reporting and cancellation calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Price urged followers to 'report O'Reilly's Instagram page for bullying' and said 'I prey he gets cancelled for EVERYTHING.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames public reporting and calls for cancellation as legitimate accountability tools when content targets vulnerable individuals; guidance implies activists/complainants should use platform reporting and public pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable work or parenthood does not excuse offensive jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Article notes the comedian 'does charity football games for children and sure he has his own kids.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of charitable activities or having children is not presented as a mitigating factor that justifies making discriminatory jokes; evaluators should not accept philanthropy as an excuse for harmful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy 'crosses a line' when it targets vulnerable individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece: 'such jokes cross a line, particularly when they involve vulnerable individuals like her son.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider the vulnerability of targets; jokes that punch down at those unable to defend themselves are flagged as crossing ethical boundaries and deserving of criticism or sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat disability-targeting jokes as a form of discrimination meriting accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Price 'has consistently framed the issue as one of discrimination, urging for greater accountability in entertainment and media.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where humour targets disability, it should be assessed through an anti-discrimination lens and may justify demands for industry or platform accountability, policy changes, or sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance: preserve space for risky, boundary-pushing comedy (countervailing criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shane Allen, Head of Comedy for Channel 4, defended airing the show: 'We think that it is important that a space on terrestrial TV exists for comedy that takes risks and pushes boundaries and we stand by our original decision to broadcast the programme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters may legitimately weigh the value of risk-taking and boundary-pushing in comedy against potential harm; editorial policies should balance creative freedom and public sensitivity rather than defaulting to censorship.
